newsitem.title: CHILE: Cesar Mendoza, ex-member of Chilean junta, dies.
newsitem.headline: Cesar Mendoza, ex-member of Chilean junta, dies.

text.p: Police Gen. Cesar Mendoza, a member of the Chilean military junta that took power in a 1973 coup, died early on Friday at the age of 79, hospital spokesmen said.

Mendoza and military president Gen. Augusto Pinochet worked closely together as members of the four-man junta that took power in Chile on Sept. 11, 1973, after a coup led by Pinochet overthrew socialist President Salvador Allende.
Mendoza represented the Carabineros national police force on the junta.

He had been operated on for cancer in June but his condition declined and led to liver failure, police hospital director Rolando Ramirez told reporters. State television said he suffered from pancreatic cancer.
His death followed by two weeks the death of another military junta member, Adm. Jose Toribio Merino, on Aug. 30.

Mendoza's moment of greatest notoriety came in 1985, when he was forced to resign from the junta after Carabinero police were accused of the kidnapping and brutal murder of three communists. The three were abducted in broad daylight during a wave of protests against Pinochet's government and found the next day with their throats slit.

The so-called "cutthroats case" became permamently linked to Mendoza's name. He was the only junta member never known to have had serious disagreements or power struggles with Pinochet and he had a reputation as a coolheaded confidant of the president, who ruled Chile until 1990.
Mendoza, married and with two children, was a talented horseman who won a bronze medal with the Chilean equestrian team at the Helsinki Olympics in 1952.
